title: [v0.4.27] Epic: make developer access and profiles portable
author: mcpdev80
body:
Parent: #874 · Final acceptance: #174
Contract freeze: #175
Related: #408, #613, #743, #399, #61, #102

## Goal

Freeze one simple, standards-first developer access and credential-portability model before v0.5.

BaseHarbor must work locally without requiring a BaseHarbor login. Existing native authentication is always preferred. BaseHarbor-managed credentials are an opt-in convenience/security feature, not a prerequisite for normal development.

> **As little as possible, as much as necessary.**
>
> **Native standards first. BaseHarbor manages credentials only when useful or explicitly requested.**

This issue also defines portable developer-profile export/import and its boundary to application backup/restore and platform disaster recovery.

---

## Developer UX first

This issue is governed by the product principle:

> **As little as possible, as much as necessary.**
>
> **Developer UX first: BaseHarbor should make the secure and correct path feel like the easy path.**

The normal developer must not need to understand BaseHarbor internals, OpenBao placement, certificate mechanics, OIDC client parameters, provider administration, Target-access plumbing or recovery internals merely to get work done.

### UX rules

- Prefer automatic discovery and reuse over asking questions.
- Prefer one sensible default over presenting multiple equivalent choices.
- Ask only when BaseHarbor cannot safely infer the answer.
- Keep advanced controls hidden until explicitly requested or actually required.
- Never make the developer repeat information BaseHarbor already knows.
- Never require repeated credential entry when a safe reusable identity/session/device enrollment already exists.
- Use guided flows for setup, import, access changes, removal and recovery.
- Wizards show only the decision needed at the current step; do not front-load architecture or security questionnaires.
- Destructive operations show impact and default to the narrowest safe action.
- Machine/automation surfaces expose the same semantics without interactive prompts.
- Error messages explain what failed and give one concrete next action instead of exposing implementation detail.
- Local development stays zero-ceremony where safe.
- Dev Remote should be one-time enrollment/import followed by normal work.
- Shared/Test/Prod may require stronger identity and authorization, but the developer experience must remain as compact as the policy permits.

### Happy-path expectation

For common workflows, the intended experience is approximately:

```text
Dev Local
  -> clone/open repo
  -> baha app init
  -> baha up
```

and:

```text
Dev Remote
  -> receive enrollment bundle
  -> baha import <bundle>
  -> baha up
```

The developer should not have to manually configure CA files, issuer URLs, client IDs, OpenBao credentials, provider tokens or remote-runtime plumbing in the normal path.

For shared/team environments:

```text
receive connection profile
  -> import
  -> authenticate when policy requires it
  -> work
```

### Acceptance

- [ ] Every normal onboarding/offboarding flow has a documented happy path with the minimum possible number of human decisions.
- [ ] No wizard asks for information already discoverable from the selected installation, profile, native toolchain or current state.
- [ ] Advanced authentication, trust and provider details are progressively disclosed rather than shown by default.
- [ ] Repeated daily developer operations do not require repeated login/credential prompts while valid reusable access exists.
- [ ] Dev Local and trusted Dev Remote remain materially simpler than shared/Test/Prod operation.
- [ ] CLI wording and Console flows optimize for developer intent first, implementation detail second.

---

## Core UX contract

### Local development: no login required

The normal local path remains:

```text
git clone <repo>
cd <repo>
baha app init
baha up
```

No `baha login` is required merely to:

- initialize or inspect an application;
- use Docker or Podman;
- use a local K3s target when existing access already works;
- use an existing Git checkout;
- clone/fetch/push through existing Git authentication;
- use local BaseHarbor-managed providers.

BaseHarbor login/authentication is introduced only where the developer or target policy requires it.

Typical examples:

- BaseHarbor Web Console;
- explicitly protected test/prod targets;
- centrally managed credentials;
- remote organizational control planes;
- approval/audit workflows requiring a human identity.

Do not turn optional security capabilities into mandatory onboarding ceremony.

---

## Repository workspace location

When BaseHarbor itself clones or creates developer-visible Git repositories, the default workspace root is:

```text
~/baseharbor/repos/
```

Repository paths should be deterministic and human-readable:

```text
~/baseharbor/repos/<host>/<owner-or-group>/<repository>
```

Examples:

```text
~/baseharbor/repos/github.com/mcpdev80/baseharbor
~/baseharbor/repos/gitlab.example.com/platform/backend
```

Rules:

- existing local repositories remain valid and do not have to be moved;
- developer-local paths remain outside portable Application Intent;
- BaseHarbor internal state still uses the appropriate XDG/config/state/cache locations rather than polluting the visible repository tree;
- the workspace model from #613 remains authoritative for Git state and safe synchronization.

---

## Native authentication first

BaseHarbor MUST reuse existing standard/native authentication before proposing BaseHarbor-managed credentials.

### Git

Use the installed/native Git client and its normal authentication chain, including as applicable:

- Git credential helpers;
- Git Credential Manager/platform-native credential stores;
- SSH agent;
- `~/.ssh/config`;
- HTTPS token/basic authentication already configured for Git;
- client certificate/mTLS configuration supported by the native Git/HTTP stack.

Hard rule:

```text
If normal git works, BaseHarbor should not ask the developer to configure Git credentials again.
```

#613 remains the Git/workspace authority. This issue extends the surrounding credential-source and portability model; it does not replace Git authentication or introduce a proprietary Git client.

### Kubernetes / K3s / OpenShift / OKD

For remote/runtime access prefer the standard Kubernetes client configuration chain:

- `KUBECONFIG`;
- `~/.kube/config`;
- selected/current context;
- exec credential plugins;
- OIDC where configured;
- client certificate authentication where configured.

BaseHarbor must not require a second credential model merely because a target is managed through BaseHarbor.

### Cloud

Where applicable, use provider-standard credential chains first, such as:

- AWS profiles / credential chain / SSO / workload identity;
- Azure CLI / managed or workload identity;
- Google ADC / gcloud / workload identity.

Exact provider implementation belongs to the later runtime/provider tracks. The pre-freeze contract is that native access mechanisms remain first-class and are not replaced by a mandatory BaseHarbor login.

---

## Minimal credential choice

Do not present a credential-management questionnaire.

If existing native authentication succeeds, continue silently.

Only when authentication is required and cannot be satisfied automatically should BaseHarbor ask for the minimum needed information.

After the developer supplies credential material, the normal human choice should remain conceptually this small:

```text
Store securely for future use?
[Yes] [No]
```

Meaning:

### No — session only

- credential is available only to the current operation/session;
- do not write it into Git or portable intent;
- do not persist it into OpenBao;
- temporary secret-bearing files use a protected per-user runtime directory where needed, e.g. `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/baseharbor/` / `/run/user/<uid>/baseharbor/`;
- owner-only permissions;
- remove temporary material when the session/operation ends;
- prefer in-memory/stdin/agent mechanisms over temporary files where supported.

### Yes — secure durable storage

- credential becomes BaseHarbor-managed protected state;
- OpenBao is the authoritative durable secret source where the selected local/remote BaseHarbor deployment provides managed secrets;
- portable/declarative state stores only references and non-secret metadata;
- runtime files/env/native secrets are projections only, consistent with #743;
- later use should be automatic and should not repeatedly prompt the developer;
- rotation/revocation must not require rewriting portable Application Intent.

Do not expose OpenBao implementation details in the normal prompt.

---

## Credential classes in scope

The underlying model may support at least:

- username/password;
- bearer/API/PAT token;
- SSH private key + optional passphrase;
- client certificate/private key + CA/trust for mTLS;
- repository/registry robot/service credentials;
- external OIDC/OAuth client material where appropriate.

Human login factors such as MFA/TOTP/Passkeys/WebAuthn belong to the human identity provider/session, not to a generic repository secret KV model.

Machine identities such as AppRole/workload identity remain distinct from human identity and external-resource credentials.

The UI/CLI should expose these distinctions only when required by the selected authentication mechanism.

---

## Local vs remote secret ownership

### Local target

Typical runtimes:

```text
Docker
Podman
occasionally local K3s
```

For a local BaseHarbor deployment, securely stored BaseHarbor-managed credentials may live in the local OpenBao/protected-state boundary.

They are eligible for explicit secure developer-profile export/import and local disaster-recovery backup according to the rules below.

### Remote target

Typical runtimes:

```text
K3s
Kubernetes
OpenShift / OKD
cloud runtime/provider
```

When the BaseHarbor control plane/secret store lives on the remote target:

- target-side secrets remain on the target by default;
- a normal developer-profile export MUST NOT silently download remote secret material;
- another developer machine should normally reconnect using the standard target access mechanism;
- explicit backup/disaster-recovery of the remote BaseHarbor platform is a separate operation from developer-profile portability.

Hard rule:

```text
Secrets live where they are needed.
Developer profile portability must not become accidental secret replication.
```

---

## Developer profile export/import

Provide a versioned, provider-neutral profile portability model for moving a developer setup between machines.

Conceptually:

```text
baha export
baha import <bundle>
```

Exact final CLI placement/naming remains subject to #603 CLI consolidation, but the semantic capability must exist before freeze.

### Default export

The default export contains only non-secret developer/baseharbor profile state that is safe and useful to recreate the local setup, such as where applicable:

- registered repository/source definitions;
- developer-local workspace mappings;
- target definitions that are safe to move;
- selected contexts/preferences;
- non-secret trust/config references;
- credential references without secret values;
- schema/version metadata.

It MUST NOT silently export:

- passwords/tokens/private keys;
- OpenBao root/recovery/unseal material;
- runtime bearer tokens;
- short-lived mTLS identities;
- remote-target secret contents.

### Secure export with credentials

An explicit opt-in may include eligible locally managed durable credentials.

Requirements:

- encrypted portable bundle;
- authenticated encryption;
- strong KDF when protected by a user passphrase;
- passphrase/key never appears in process arguments or logs;
- bundle is integrity protected and versioned;
- no plaintext secret archive is written as an intermediate normal path;
- import validates version/integrity before mutation;
- imported secrets are written back into the destination protected/OpenBao store rather than becoming a second plaintext source of truth;
- conflict handling is explicit and fail-closed;
- secret values are never shown in normal output/evidence.

UX should remain minimal, e.g.:

```text
Include securely stored local credentials?
[Yes] [No]
```

Do not present cryptographic implementation choices unless the user explicitly requests advanced control.

---

## Multi-device behavior

Two supported patterns:

### Independent local development machines

Each machine may have:

- its own local runtime;
- its own local BaseHarbor protected/OpenBao state;
- its own `~/baseharbor/repos/` workspace.

Use export/import only when the developer wants to move BaseHarbor-managed local profile/credentials.

Native Git/cloud/kube authentication that already exists on the destination machine should continue to be reused rather than overwritten.

### Shared remote BaseHarbor target

Multiple developer machines connect to the same target.

Target-side managed credentials remain centralized on the target. Each developer machine only needs its own standard access/session identity.

Do not replicate target secrets merely to make a second workstation usable.

---

## Export/import != backup/restore

These are distinct lifecycle semantics.

### Developer profile export/import

Purpose:

```text
move/recreate my developer setup on another machine
```

Focus:

- developer-local configuration;
- workspace/repository mappings;
- target references;
- optional explicitly selected locally managed credentials.

### Application backup/restore

Owned by #399 / #61.

Purpose:

```text
recover application durable state
```

Do not merge the application Recovery Unit with developer-profile portability.

### Platform / BaseHarbor disaster recovery

Purpose:

```text
recover the BaseHarbor control plane / target itself
```

This includes the protected secret-store recovery story where applicable and remains distinct from a normal developer export.

The contracts may reuse common encrypted archive primitives, but MUST NOT become one ambiguous `backup everything` operation.

---

## Backup and recoverability of secure local credentials

Choosing `secure` must not create unrecoverable hidden state.

Requirements:

- BaseHarbor-managed durable local credentials participate in the supported local platform/recovery strategy;
- OpenBao data backup and the required recovery/seal material are treated as separate security assets;
- recovery material is never silently embedded next to the only backup copy;
- restoration verifies that the secret store is usable before reporting success;
- short-lived/generated runtime identities should normally be regenerated rather than exported/restored as authoritative credentials;
- external credentials that cannot be restored safely must be reported explicitly rather than silently omitted.

---

## Console behavior

The Web Console is an authenticated management surface.

The Console may allow creation/use of repository, registry, artifact and target credentials, but uses the same core credential-source model as CLI/JSON/MCP.

No Console-only credential database.

When a user chooses secure storage through the Console:

```text
non-secret configuration/reference -> declarative/profile state
secret material                    -> protected/OpenBao state
```

The Console should not require the developer to understand the storage implementation.

---

## Repository / artifact consumers

The same credential-source semantics must be reusable by external resources without creating product-specific credential systems, including conceptually:

- Git repositories;
- OCI/container registries;
- Harbor / Quay / GHCR and compatible registries;
- Artifactory / Nexus;
- Helm repositories;
- Maven/npm/PyPI/raw artifact sources;
- future provider/distribution sources.

This issue freezes the access/credential-source boundary, not every product integration.

---

## Security rules

- no secret value in portable Application Intent;
- no plaintext secret committed to Git;
- no secret value in normal logs/status/doctor/evidence;
- do not persist temporary credentials when the user chose session-only;
- prefer native OS/Git/SSH/kube/cloud mechanisms when already working;
- do not weaken TLS/authentication to avoid a prompt;
- do not copy remote target secrets to a developer machine by default;
- do not require a BaseHarbor account/login for ordinary local development;
- BaseHarbor-managed credentials must have explicit ownership, scope and revocation/rotation semantics;
- imported bundles must be treated as untrusted input until format/integrity validation succeeds.

---

## CLI / JSON / MCP / Console parity

All surfaces use one shared domain model for:

- credential source;
- persistence choice;
- target/local ownership;
- exportability;
- import result/conflict;
- secret-safe diagnostics.

Presentation differs, semantics do not.

MCP/automation must not receive raw secret values merely because the human CLI can interactively provide them.

Secret-taking operations must use safe input channels and explicit sensitivity metadata.

---

## Acceptance

### Frictionless local development

- [ ] Clean local Docker/Podman developer journey works without `baha login`.
- [ ] Existing Git credential helper authentication is reused without extra prompts.
- [ ] Existing SSH-agent/config authentication is reused without extra prompts.
- [ ] Existing local repository can be adopted without moving it.
- [ ] BaseHarbor-created clone defaults to `~/baseharbor/repos/<host>/<owner-or-group>/<repo>`.

### Runtime/target standards first

- [ ] Existing kubeconfig/context works without creating duplicate BaseHarbor credentials.
- [ ] Kubernetes exec/OIDC/client-cert authentication can remain authoritative.
- [ ] Architecture allows cloud-native credential chains without requiring a BaseHarbor-specific cloud login contract.
- [ ] Native access failure produces actionable guidance before offering managed storage.

### Temporary credentials

- [ ] Session-only credential is not persisted in Git, portable intent or OpenBao.
- [ ] Temporary secret files, if unavoidable, are owner-only and cleaned up.
- [ ] Normal output/logs do not expose the credential.

### Secure credentials

- [ ] Secure choice persists eligible credential material in the authoritative protected/OpenBao store.
- [ ] Future operations can reuse it without repeated credential prompts.
- [ ] Only references/non-secret metadata enter declarative/profile state.
- [ ] Rotation/revocation preserves the same repository/target logical reference.
- [ ] Secure local credentials are recoverable through the supported recovery model.

### Export/import

- [ ] Default export contains no secret values.
- [ ] Secure credential export requires explicit opt-in.
- [ ] Secret-bearing export is encrypted, authenticated and versioned.
- [ ] Import validates before mutation.
- [ ] Import restores secret material into the protected destination store.
- [ ] Conflicts are explicit and fail closed.
- [ ] Remote target secrets are not silently exported.
- [ ] Multi-device local setup can be recreated without requiring manual BaseHarbor state surgery.

### Lifecycle boundaries

- [ ] Developer profile export/import is documented separately from #399 Application Recovery Unit.
- [ ] Platform disaster recovery is not conflated with profile export.
- [ ] Short-lived runtime identities are regenerated rather than treated as portable developer credentials where appropriate.
- [ ] Recovery/seal material is handled separately from ordinary exported secrets.

### UX

- [ ] Existing authentication success causes no credential questionnaire.
- [ ] When input is required, the normal persistence choice is no more complex than secure-for-future-use vs session-only.
- [ ] Advanced authentication types/options appear only when needed.
- [ ] Human wording follows “as little as possible, as much as necessary.”

### Cross-surface

- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP/Console consume the same credential-source semantics.
- [ ] Machine surfaces remain secret-safe.
- [ ] No Console-only credential database or CLI-only credential behavior exists.

---

## Pre-freeze rule

This issue is a blocker for #174 semantic acceptance and #175 contract freeze.

The v0.5 baseline MUST NOT freeze any of these accidental assumptions:

- BaseHarbor login is required for local development;
- BaseHarbor replaces Git/SSH/kubeconfig/cloud-native authentication;
- developer profile export is equivalent to application backup;
- remote target secrets are copied to developer machines by default;
- securely stored local credentials are impossible to back up/recover;
- repository credentials require a product-specific credential model.

The frozen rule is:

```text
native standards first
  -> work without BaseHarbor login when safe
  -> ask only when necessary
  -> developer chooses temporary vs secure persistence
  -> secure means reusable + protected + recoverable
  -> secrets stay at their proper ownership boundary
```


## Clarification: simple shared-team Target onboarding and external corporate SSO

Planning clarification from 2026-10-06. This belongs to this existing v0.4.25 issue; it does not expand v0.4.22 or change its running pre-release. #803 is consolidated here.

### Developer UX

Platform administrator configures the team destination once; a new colleague receives a non-secret Target reference/profile, reuses native access, signs in through the existing corporate IdP only when needed, then works. No repeated issuer/client-ID/OpenBao questionnaire, shared administrator token, mandatory managed Keycloak, or Baha user directory.

Attaching to an existing Target and administrator bootstrap are separate. Attach never creates a second OpenBao/Keycloak. Corporate client registration/consent/redirects/claims remain an administrator prerequisite; Baha automates only owned resources with granted rights and explains any missing prerequisite with one concrete next action.

### Required semantics to settle and prove

- External OIDC is a complete path without managed Keycloak; operator identity remains independent from application identity.
- Trusted-local is limited to the established local trust boundary. Shared/remote dev still requires authenticated, scoped authorization; changing the environment label cannot grant local trust.
- Verified issuer + subject and configured stable group/app-role claims map to the existing operation/policy model and Target/scope/app/environment bounds. Being logged into corporate SSO does not grant team access.
- Read/log, deploy/change, secret use/write, secret reveal, destroy and platform administration have distinct permissions where supported. No new IAM framework; later JIT/break-glass/approvals remain #100.
- Reuse native kubeconfig/context/credential plugins. Kubernetes authentication, Baha operator authorization and OpenBao permissions remain separate; tokens have service-specific validation and audience.
- Resolve the correct secret store through authoritative remote provider placement, including TLS trust and app/environment secret scope. Multiple Targets/scopes may share a store with separate permissions. Never use local/default OpenBao as fallback when the remote store fails.
- Ordinary app operations use authorized Core paths and target-side scoped machine identities; no human OpenBao manager/root/AppRole credential is distributed. Direct human OpenBao management is optional and separately authorized.
- Define private/ClusterIP store reachability without assuming laptop access or requiring an unprotected ingress.
- Two developer machines/local aliases must refer to one stable shared destination and authoritative target-side deployment/provider state. Local metadata is reference/cache state. Concurrent mutation, shared-provider creation and stale revisions need a bounded conflict/coordination rule using existing Core mechanisms.
- Target references/discovery are non-secret, versioned and trust-verified. Import must not redirect credentials, execute untrusted native plugins or overwrite working native authentication.
- Reuse valid sessions; do not promise exactly one browser redirect despite IdP MFA/consent policies. Define bounded authorization staleness, expiry/revalidation and supported token/session revocation; group removal or IdP logout does not instantly invalidate every already-issued token.
- Default profile export never copies remote secrets.

### Review findings, not completed implementation

Current operator OIDC verification supports external issuers. However, the reviewed common principal projection lacks configurable group/role authorization claims; the shared authorization boundary does not establish team membership/resource permission by verifying identity alone. Current dev classification is environment-based, and the bootstrap choice defaults to managed Keycloak. Existing target and HTTP contracts alone do not prove two-client remote state authority.

These findings must be resolved/proven for this scope; closed #769/#770 remain delivered foundations, not proof of the complete team scenario. #100 currently includes deferred group/role mapping: clarify the minimum team-access prerequisite here before freeze while advanced governance stays later.

### Additional acceptance

- [ ] Local Docker/Podman works without login while shared remote dev denies anonymous/forged trusted-local access.
- [ ] New team member attaches the configured Target and uses external corporate SSO without managed Keycloak or per-user provider setup.
- [ ] Authenticated nonmember is denied; mapped developer cannot access another team/prod, reveal secrets or administer providers without permission.
- [ ] Wrong issuer/tenant/audience, missing/overage claims and expired sessions fail closed with actionable output.
- [ ] Same app on local and remote Targets uses different secret values correctly; no cross-target fallback or profile secret replication.
- [ ] Private secret-store access works through the supported access path without distributing manager credentials.
- [ ] Two clients observe one remote deployment/provider identity and safe conflicting-update behavior.
- [ ] Offboarding respects documented expiry/revalidation/revocation bounds.
- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP/HTTP share decisions and actor attribution; onboarding is separate from bootstrap.
- [ ] Pre-freeze Core/HTTP/contract-fixture evidence is explicitly separated from real Kubernetes lifecycle implementation/acceptance in #102 (v0.7) and #320 (v0.8).

Checked primary references:
- https://openbao.org/docs/auth/jwt/
- https://openbao.org/docs/concepts/tokens/
- https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/develop/configure-tokens-group-claims-app-roles


## Managed Identity: central administration of BaseHarbor's own access

Confirmed scope (2026-10-06): a team may use BaseHarbor as its central tool from the outset, including administering BaseHarbor access through the authentication service BaseHarbor already manages. This is a supported alternative to external corporate SSO, not merely an external-SSO integration or a general-purpose company IAM system.

### Scope and developer UX

Reuse the existing managed Identity provider (Keycloak reference implementation). No second user database, mandatory external IdP, or separate authentication service is introduced.

The normal administrator journey is:
1. Select an existing user or create/invite a new user in the managed authentication service.
2. Assign a BaseHarbor team/organization access profile that references one or more Targets and the permitted BaseHarbor operations/scopes/environments.
3. Provide a minimal onboarding profile/reference; the colleague activates their account through the authentication service, configures password/MFA there where required, imports/attaches the profile and works.
4. Change or revoke BaseHarbor access within the selected independent installation/security boundary.

Keep the normal flow compact. Reuse existing role recommendations/policy and organization/profile composition from #608/#609; do not introduce another mandatory role taxonomy or an IAM questionnaire. Non-secret configuration/profile assignment is not itself an authorization grant: effective permissions are enforced centrally.

A versioned onboarding file/reference may carry organization/team configuration, Target/access references, trust information and authentication metadata. It does not normally contain passwords, existing sessions, OpenBao manager/root credentials or remote application secrets. Secure local credential export remains the separate explicit option defined above. Any invitation/enrollment capability, if used, must have recipient binding, bounded lifetime, replay protection and supported revocation; copying a profile must not grant another identity access.

### Architecture and ownership

Use the existing protected management surface:

CLI / Console / MCP / management HTTP
 -> shared Core authentication, authorization, policy and audit
 -> Identity Capability Provider management adapter
 -> managed authentication service's supported native administration interface

For the Keycloak reference provider, use its Admin REST API with least-privilege protected provider credentials. Other managed Identity providers advertise the bounded administration capabilities they actually support; missing capability or permission produces an actionable result, never a hidden provider shell/API bypass.

These are management operations, not operations of the Application Runtime REST API. That API remains scoped to application runtime functions. Provider administrator tokens remain internal and never reach developers or ordinary machine results.

The managed authentication service remains authoritative for user accounts, credentials, password activation/reset, MFA and authentication sessions. BaseHarbor manages only its own access relationships, profiles and provider-owned integration resources. Application/business-user administration and unrelated applications are outside this scope and remain available through the provider's own UI.

Account creation/invitation is explicit and idempotent; existing users are resolved by stable provider identity and ambiguity fails closed. Access administration requires separately authorized administrative permission. Removing BaseHarbor access removes its owned grants and applies the documented session/token revocation rules; it never silently deletes a shared identity or unrelated memberships. Reuse the offboarding/staleness requirements above.

### Planning boundary

This minimal BaseHarbor-access workflow belongs to #777 / v0.4.25 and reuses #770/#767/#769. Advanced JIT, approvals, break-glass and general privileged-access governance remain #100; do not defer the minimal managed-user onboarding/access assignment solely because #100 contains advanced identity/governance work.

No implementation or additional scope is added to v0.4.22 or its running pre-release by this clarification.

### Acceptance

- [ ] A team using the existing BaseHarbor-managed Identity service can create/invite a colleague, assign an access profile and onboard them without external SSO.
- [ ] Profiles reuse organization/team configuration and support one or multiple Targets with explicit operation/scope/environment permissions.
- [ ] Account activation/password/MFA stays with the authentication service; no copied administrator token or second user database is needed.
- [ ] Provider management capabilities/permissions are checked before mutation; unsupported administration is actionable.
- [ ] Repeated onboarding is idempotent; ambiguous existing identities are rejected.
- [ ] Non-admin users cannot create users or grant/revoke access; profile tampering/import cannot elevate permissions.
- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP/HTTP share Core authorization and provider-adapter behavior; Console has no independent identity/access store.
- [ ] Management operations are excluded from the Application Runtime REST API.
- [ ] Onboarding profile/reference contains no default secret/session export; any enrollment capability has the stated lifetime/recipient/replay protections.
- [ ] Access change/revocation is verified against effective permissions and documented stale-session bounds; unrelated identity/provider resources survive.
- [ ] General account/business-user administration for other applications remains out of scope.


## Authority and topology: independent installations per security boundary (2026-10-06)

Confirmed architecture decision: BaseHarbor may be the central management tool within a security boundary. Dev and Prod use independent installations; no global BaseHarbor authority, Baha-to-Baha communication, federation, registry synchronization or cross-installation reconciliation is required.

This replaces the earlier open-ended central-authority proposal. It is planned scope within #777 / v0.4.25, not completed functionality or a scope change for v0.4.22.

### Keep Target and management connection distinct

A Target remains a runtime provider + access reference + scope under the existing Target contract. A management connection identifies the Core endpoint responsible for operations; it is not a replacement Target definition or a new application environment.

One management installation may own multiple explicitly admitted Targets inside its security boundary. A separate Core is not required for every namespace/Target. Independent local development remains self-contained and requires no remote management service or login.

Current #408 configuration/state is user/installation-local; #608 distributes versioned organization configuration; #767 is a protected HTTP projection over the existing Core. None of these alone proves complete remote onboarding, an authoritative shared directory or client delegation. Implement and verify the missing behavior through the existing Core/contracts rather than introducing a separate control-plane product or duplicating lifecycle logic.

### Ownership and isolation

- Each independent installation owns its registered Target references, BaseHarbor access profiles/assignments, deployment/provider authority and explicit secret-store mappings for its admitted scope.
- Dev has no management access, credentials or implicit trust for Prod; neither installation queries, forwards requests to or synchronizes with the other. No installation implicitly discovers or administers unrelated installations.
- Each managed deployment/resource set has one authoritative Core owner. Local client metadata is reference/cache state, never a competing writable deployment or authorization database.
- The managed Identity service remains authoritative for accounts, credentials, MFA and sessions. BaseHarbor owns its Target metadata and BaseHarbor access-policy mappings, without another user database or a Target registry hidden in IdP attributes.
- For the strictly isolated managed-Identity topology, use independent auth services/trust and protected secret-store boundaries. A Dev-owned identity or secret service must not become a Prod dependency. No automatic user, session, grant or secret synchronization.
- External/shared IdP support remains the separate supported option above; common identity does not merge installation authority, grant access or relax network isolation.
- Secret-store selection is explicit and authoritative within the selected installation and Target/provider scope. Multiple admitted Targets may use a permitted shared store inside that boundary. Never fall back to a local, Dev, Prod or other store when the selected remote store fails.
- Runtime and provider credentials stay behind the responsible Core/access-provider boundary. Clients do not bypass Core to call the node connector or receive provider administrator credentials.
- A registered Target is not automatically authorized: native access, trust and scoped permissions must pass preflight. Admission cannot grant an installation rights over unrelated resources.
- A client can hold references to multiple installations and connect directly to each only where network policy and that installation's authorization permit it. A profile creates neither reachability nor access. Where networks are separated, use the client/Console from an authorized environment; do not introduce forwarding through Dev.

### Minimal onboarding and developer UX

Administrator, within the selected installation:
1. Create/invite or resolve the colleague through its existing managed Identity provider adapter.
2. Assign a BaseHarbor team/organization access profile for one or more admitted Targets and explicit operations/scopes/environments.
3. Provide a small versioned connection/onboarding profile or reference.

Developer:
1. Add/import the connection profile.
2. Authenticate with that installation's configured Identity service when required.
3. See permitted Targets, select one and work through the responsible Core.

Reuse the managed-Identity management API/Core/provider-adapter path above; this is not the Application Runtime REST API. Ordinary local development and direct native access remain supported under the existing trust rules.

The connection profile contains endpoint, stable installation/Target references and non-secret authentication/trust metadata. It contains no default passwords, sessions, Kubernetes administrator credentials, OpenBao tokens or remote secrets. Validate authenticity/trust and destination binding before sending credentials; import itself cannot grant rights. Do not require developers to configure OpenBao placement, issuer/client parameters or provider administration individually.

Team/company configuration can be distributed as versioned profiles using #608. A common profile is configuration, not a global live authority; it neither discovers every Target nor creates synchronized grants across installations. Target listing is filtered by the selected installation's authorization. Any client presentation of multiple known connections must preserve their distinct authority and identity.

### Access change and offboarding

Create, assign, change and revoke access per independent installation/security boundary. Access to Dev never implies access to Prod. Do not promise a global one-click grant/revocation or automatic account synchronization.

Removing access must enforce the documented revalidation/expiry/revocation bounds for that installation; do not promise immediate invalidation of all previously issued tokens merely because a group membership changed. Preserve unrelated provider identities and memberships.


### Guided removal and offboarding UX

Removal and offboarding MUST use the same guided UX principle as onboarding: the normal human path is a small wizard that explains exactly what will change, shows the affected scope, preserves unrelated resources by default and requires explicit confirmation before destructive mutation. Advanced flags remain available for automation, but normal users are not expected to memorize destructive command combinations.

The guided flow applies consistently to at least:

- BaseHarbor user/access removal;
- managed-Identity user disable/delete where BaseHarbor actually owns that identity;
- Dev Remote device/workstation revocation;
- local management-connection/profile removal;
- unused or outstanding enrollment-bundle revocation;
- Target/access-profile/grant removal where in scope.

#### User/access removal wizard

The wizard first distinguishes the intended operation:

```text
What do you want to remove?

[1] BaseHarbor access only
[2] Disable managed user
[3] Delete managed user
```

Defaults MUST favor the least destructive action.

Before confirmation it shows:

- installation/security boundary;
- stable user identity;
- affected BaseHarbor profiles, Targets and grants;
- expected session/token revocation bounds;
- whether the underlying managed Identity account is preserved, disabled or deleted;
- unrelated provider memberships/resources that will remain untouched.

Removing BaseHarbor access MUST NOT silently delete the managed Identity account. Deleting a managed user is a separate explicit operation and is only available when BaseHarbor owns/administers that account and the operator has the required permission.

#### Dev Remote device/workstation removal wizard

Each enrolled workstation/device is individually manageable. The wizard lists recognizable metadata such as device label, stable device identity, enrollment/last-seen timestamps where available, and scope without exposing credential material.

A normal removal flow is:

```text
Select device
  -> review identity and affected access
  -> revoke device
  -> terminate/reject its renewable credentials/sessions according to the supported bounds
  -> preserve every other enrolled device
```

Revoking workstation A MUST NOT revoke workstation B or delete remote deployments, Targets, provider state or application data.

#### Local connection/profile removal wizard

Removing a known management connection from one workstation is a local cleanup operation unless the user explicitly chooses a remote revocation action.

The wizard distinguishes:

```text
Remove from this workstation only
Revoke this workstation on the remote Core and remove locally
```

Local-only removal deletes local connection metadata, cached/session material and selected defaults for that installation. It MUST NOT delete the remote Core, its Targets, deployments, users, grants, secrets or provider state.

#### Enrollment-bundle lifecycle

Unused or outstanding enrollment bundles/tokens/authorizations can be listed and revoked where the selected enrollment mechanism supports server-side revocation. Successfully consumed one-time enrollment material is not treated as a reusable standing credential; the resulting device identity is managed/revoked instead.

The wizard clearly distinguishes:

- revoke unused enrollment;
- revoke enrolled device;
- remove only the local imported profile.

#### Wizard behavior

All guided destructive flows:

- show impact before mutation;
- default to the narrowest safe action;
- never infer broad deletion from a short alias;
- require explicit confirmation for irreversible identity deletion;
- support back/cancel with no mutation;
- revalidate authorization and current object state at submit time;
- fail closed on stale/deleted/ambiguous identities;
- provide one concrete recovery action on conflicts;
- produce the same semantic result through CLI, Console and machine surfaces, with prompts only on interactive surfaces.

Additional acceptance:

- [ ] An operator can remove only BaseHarbor access without deleting the underlying managed Identity user.
- [ ] Managed-user deletion is a separate explicit guided action with impact review and permission check.
- [ ] A Dev Remote workstation can be revoked independently without affecting other workstations or remote application/platform state.
- [ ] Local connection removal cannot accidentally delete or revoke the remote installation.
- [ ] The wizard distinguishes local cleanup, remote device revocation and unused enrollment revocation.
- [ ] Back/cancel and failed authorization/state revalidation produce no partial destructive mutation.

### Kubernetes planning boundary

Namespace operation is the prioritized/default mode; explicitly supported cluster-wide operation is a broader resource scope, not an exemption from authorization or a bridge between Dev and Prod. Describe native RBAC and network requirements; a namespace name alone is not a complete security boundary.

Real Kubernetes bootstrap/runtime implementation and acceptance remain in #102 (v0.7), with the broader Kubernetes track in #320 (v0.8). This issue freezes access/topology contracts and distinguishes Core/HTTP fixture evidence from real Kubernetes lifecycle evidence; it does not claim those runtime capabilities are already delivered.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Topology documents independent local/Dev/Prod authorities, their admitted Targets, identity ownership and explicit secret-store placement.
- [ ] One installation supports multiple admitted Targets without one mandatory Core per Target; Target and management connection remain distinct.
- [ ] Two authorized workstations connected to the same installation observe one authoritative deployment/provider state and the same permitted Target references, with bounded conflict handling.
- [ ] Dev and Prod need no Baha-to-Baha traffic, registry/user/grant synchronization, shared administrator credential or Dev-owned dependency.
- [ ] The client connects directly to the selected authorized Core; network isolation is not bypassed by forwarding, profile import or cached metadata.
- [ ] Managed-Identity onboarding completes through account invitation/activation, scoped profile assignment and minimal profile import without external SSO, duplicate user storage or developer OpenBao setup.
- [ ] Anonymous shared-Dev access and environment-label-based trusted-local escalation are denied.
- [ ] Target listing and all operations enforce the selected installation's identity and operation/resource scope; Dev identities/sessions/profiles cannot implicitly authorize Prod.
- [ ] Copied/tampered profiles, equal local aliases and stale client metadata do not create grants or redirect credentials to an untrusted installation.
- [ ] Wrong/unavailable remote store fails explicitly; no cross-installation store fallback or default remote-secret export occurs.
- [ ] Grant/revoke is verified independently in each boundary, including documented stale-session bounds; no global offboarding guarantee is presented.
- [ ] Standalone local Docker/Podman use still works without remote services or login; native kube/Git/cloud authentication remains first-class.
- [ ] Namespace-first and explicit cluster-wide scopes are covered by contract fixtures and linked Kubernetes requirements, without claiming completed Kubernetes runtime acceptance.
- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP/management HTTP and Console share Core policy, actor attribution and provider adapters; no independent Console identity/access store or Application Runtime management route is introduced.


---

## Developer topology: local Dev and remote Dev

Confirmed UX clarification (2026-10-06): development has two equally valid operating modes. The distinction is topology, not product edition or environment naming.

### Dev Local

The developer workstation runs the BaseHarbor Core and local runtime itself:

```text
Developer workstation
  -> baha
  -> in-process/local BaseHarbor Core
  -> local Docker/Podman/K3s Target
```

This remains the zero-ceremony default. No BaseHarbor login, onboarding file or remote management service is required merely for ordinary local development.

### Dev Remote

The developer workstation is only a client. The authoritative BaseHarbor Core and long-lived platform state run elsewhere:

```text
Developer workstation
  -> baha client
  -> remote BaseHarbor Core
       -> one or more admitted Targets
```

The remote Core may run on a VM, server, lab host or other persistent machine. "Remote Dev" does not imply production, team/shared access or Kubernetes. It simply means the developer does not run the authoritative Core locally.

The supported low-friction goal for a personally administered/trusted Dev Remote installation is:

```text
Remote BaseHarbor Core
  -> create/export one device enrollment bundle

Developer workstation
  -> baha import <dev-remote-bundle>
  -> work
```

After successful import, ordinary commands such as `baha app up`, `baha app status` and `baha app logs` MUST NOT require a browser login, username/password prompt, manual CA setup, issuer/client-ID configuration or repeated credential entry while the imported device identity remains valid.

This is explicit device enrollment for a trusted Dev Remote installation, not anonymous remote access and not the default shared-team/Test/Prod authentication model.

### Enrollment bundle semantics

A Dev Remote enrollment bundle MAY contain the protected material required to establish one pre-authorized client/device identity, in addition to non-secret connection metadata:

- Core endpoint and stable installation identity;
- authoritative TLS trust/CA material or equivalent pinned trust metadata;
- one scoped client/device identity, preferably mTLS-based;
- the minimum authorization/scope metadata needed for that device;
- expiry, rotation and revocation metadata.

The bundle MUST NOT contain Core/OpenBao root, recovery or unseal material, provider administrator credentials, remote application secrets, or unrestricted host/runtime credentials.

Because this bundle can confer access, it is secret-bearing enrollment material rather than an ordinary non-secret connection profile. Treat it as sensitive input: protected transfer, strict local permissions, validation before mutation, no logging/output of secret material, and optional source-file removal after successful import.

### Multiple developer workstations

Each workstation SHOULD receive its own independently revocable device identity even when the same person owns both machines:

```text
dev-pc-1.baha  -> device identity A
dev-pc-2.baha  -> device identity B
                     |
                     v
              same remote Dev Core
```

Both devices observe the same authoritative Core-side Target, deployment, provider and evidence state. Revoking or rotating one device MUST NOT require invalidating the other device.

Copying one already-imported workstation's runtime/session state is not the normal onboarding path. The Core should issue/export another bounded enrollment bundle for the additional workstation.

### Relationship to managed Keycloak / OIDC

The managed Identity provider remains part of the BaseHarbor Core and remains authoritative for shared-team, Test/Prod and user-centric authentication where policy requires it.

Trusted Dev Remote device enrollment is a deliberately lower-friction trust mode. A successfully imported pre-authorized device identity MAY authenticate directly to the protected Core management surface without an interactive Keycloak/OIDC login on every workstation session.

This trust mode MUST be explicitly enabled/issued by the selected installation. It MUST NOT be inferred merely from an application environment named `dev`, a Target name, or a remote network location.

### UX boundary

Normal trusted Dev Remote onboarding should be no more complex than:

```text
baha import dev-remote.baha
```

followed by normal work. Advanced trust, certificate, issuer, client or OpenBao details stay hidden unless troubleshooting or explicit advanced administration requires them.

The existing non-secret connection/onboarding profile remains the correct model for shared/team/company distribution. The Dev Remote enrollment bundle is the explicit trusted-device path where credential-bearing import is intentionally desired.

### Additional acceptance

- [ ] Dev Local works without login, onboarding bundle or remote Core.
- [ ] A fresh authorized workstation can connect to a trusted Dev Remote Core by importing one enrollment bundle and can immediately perform permitted operations without interactive login.
- [ ] Import validates Core destination/trust and bundle integrity before persisting or using credential material.
- [ ] The imported device identity is bounded, auditable, renewable and individually revocable.
- [ ] Two independently enrolled workstations can use the same Dev Remote Core and observe one authoritative remote state.
- [ ] Revoking workstation A does not revoke workstation B.
- [ ] No Core/OpenBao recovery/root material, provider administrator credential or remote application secret is included in the enrollment bundle.
- [ ] Secret-bearing import material is never emitted into logs, evidence, normal machine output or portable Application Intent.
- [ ] Trusted Dev Remote cannot be selected merely by naming an environment `dev`; it requires explicit installation policy/enrollment.
- [ ] Shared-team/Test/Prod onboarding continues to use authenticated user/session flows and does not inherit this trusted-device shortcut.


## Core capability consistency

The BaseHarbor Core product definition is fixed as:

```text
SQL + Secrets + Identity
```

Identity is therefore a Core capability, not an optional add-on. This does **not** mean every local developer must perform an interactive Identity login.

Dev Local may remain zero-login for ordinary local work, while the Core still owns the Identity capability. Shared/team/Test/Prod and user-centric management flows use that capability according to policy.

SQL, Secrets and Identity placement may be shared within the installation/security boundary or isolated for an application where policy requires stronger separation. Do not assume one shared provider instance for every application.


## v0.4.24 Core/Node/CLI handoff clarification (2026-10-09)

Reference implementation/evidence: #837 (Core and provider lifecycle), #846 (human CLI and remote Node), #849 (integration). This issue must test the **final shipped commands and identities**, not reimplement their v0.4.24 transport or upgrade code.

- [ ] Import/enrollment binds the local developer device to one **explicitly selected management Core** without treating that Core as a deployment Target. `baha use` selects the intended context; application placement remains a separate Target decision with deterministic explicit-argument precedence.
- [ ] A portable developer profile/enrollment bundle holds only Core/Target references, scope, public trust anchors and revocable device credentials as explicitly permitted; never exports OpenBao unseal keys, Keycloak provider-admin credentials, live SQL backups, etcd DCS snapshots or Patroni state.
- [ ] Local Dev remains usable without BaseHarbor login. Dev Remote uses Core-authorized device enrollment, scoped mTLS and optional organization OIDC; reconnect/renew/revoke/offboard must follow the existing #846 Node/Target-access contracts, not a duplicate credential engine.
- [ ] Test a **revoked/expired/imported-into-wrong-Core** profile, foreign installation and multi-Core selection as negatives; fail closed with a secret-safe reason and concrete next action.
- [ ] Separate export/import for developer convenience from **service backup/restore and disaster recovery**. Provider recovery in #837/#845/#847/#848 remains installation-owned and requires independent verification; profile import is not a substitute.
- [ ] Human wizard, noninteractive CLI, JSON and MCP must expose the same resolved authority, ownership, allowed next action and remediation. Console consumption does not introduce a second management authority.

No second Core/Target abstraction, no compatibility aliases for obsolete pre-freeze CLI forms, and no requirement to ship a new HA or provider upgrade engine in v0.4.25.


---

## Release assignment update (2026-10-10)
Execution belongs to **v0.4.27 #874, Session 2**. Contract definitions (portable profile import/export schema, boundaries and authority) must be specified under **v0.4.25 #872** first. The pre-existing v0.4.25 mention/parent #174 is historic; #174 now owns v0.4.31 final acceptance. Console UX/functional proof is v0.4.28 #875. No new duplicate authority. Two sessions, isolated file ownership, real Dev Local/Remote acceptance.

comments.body:
## Guided team/access profile creation and selection UX

Planning addition requested on 2026-10-06; part of v0.4.25, with no implementation or v0.4.22 pre-release scope change. This is a team/access-profile wizard, distinct from the existing Stack Profile wizard. Final command placement/names follow #603; organization configuration/distribution follows #608.

### Minimal administrator journey

1. Use the selected Baha management connection. Always show its installation and security boundary; ask to select a connection only when none is selected or the choice is ambiguous.
2. Enter the profile name.
3. Select one or more already registered Targets belonging to this installation.
4. Choose permitted Baha actions using concise role/preset suggestions with a plain-language permission summary. Permit different rights per Target when needed; expose fine-grained customization progressively rather than asking a full permissions questionnaire.
5. Review installation, profile, selected Targets and effective permissions, then confirm creation.

Creating a profile does not automatically assign users or grant access. Afterwards offer one optional next action to assign an existing identity/group or use the managed-Identity invitation flow; show the resulting grants before applying them. A separate optional connection-profile export contains references/trust metadata only and cannot grant rights.

### Lists and multi-selection

- Use readable names plus a compact distinguishing context: installation/security boundary, runtime and namespace/resource scope as appropriate. Stable IDs are available in details, not required memorization.
- For small lists, show the choices directly. For long lists, support search/filter, keyboard navigation and bounded/paged results; do not dump an unbounded wall of Targets.
- Target selection supports clear checked/unchecked state, multiple selections, selected count and an inspectable selected-items summary. Selections survive filtering and pagination and remain removable without restarting.
- Do not preselect every Target or broad permissions. Any select-all action must state whether it affects visible/filtered results; never silently include hidden or unauthorized items.
- Only list Targets the actor may view; selecting a Target does not imply authority to grant rights. Explain unavailable actions without leaking unauthorized resources.
- Display namespace and cluster-wide scope distinctly. The wizard cannot implicitly enlarge a Target's scope; broad grants require an explicit review.
- Empty lists offer one actionable next step to register/attach an eligible Target, subject to permissions. Distinguish empty, no search matches, access denied and unavailable connection.
- Back navigation preserves inputs; cancellation makes no changes. Validation errors appear at the relevant field/step and permit correction.
- Console controls have accessible labels, visible focus and keyboard support. Interactive CLI documents controls; non-interactive/unsupported terminals receive an actionable explicit-input path rather than a hanging prompt.

### Shared behavior and acceptance

CLI, Console and machine surfaces use the same Core profile validation, authorization and management operations. JSON/MCP use explicit structured inputs without interactive prompts. Revalidate selected Targets and grant authority at submission; stale/deleted Targets or changed permissions must not create partial or broader grants. Surface conflicts with one concrete recovery action and preserve the user's draft.

- [ ] An authorized administrator creates a scoped team/access profile through name → Target multi-selection → rights → review, without provider/OpenBao configuration questions.
- [ ] Small, large and duplicate-name Target lists remain usable; search, keyboard selection, pagination and preserved selections are demonstrated.
- [ ] Effective rights per selected Target, installation identity and namespace/cluster-wide scope are clear before confirmation.
- [ ] Back/cancel, empty/no-match/denied/offline states and stale selection conflicts have actionable behavior and no unintended mutation.
- [ ] Profile creation, identity/group assignment and connection-profile export remain distinct; file import cannot confer server-side rights.
- [ ] Dev profile creation cannot enumerate or grant Prod access through another independent installation.
- [ ] Suggested roles/presets are understandable defaults, not a second identity directory or mandatory provider-specific role scheme.
- [ ] CLI and Console demonstrate the same wizard semantics; JSON/MCP execute the equivalent validated operation without prompts.
